subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the spec.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for GCSE Geography simply, with an example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: What is the correct first stage of the geographical enquiry process?
options: Identifying an aim or hypothesis to investigate
questions.explain: The enquiry begins by deciding on a clear aim, question or hypothesis; the later stages (planning, collecting, presenting, analysing, concluding, evaluating) follow from it.

questions.q: Which of these is a well-worded, testable HYPOTHESIS?
options: The river's velocity increases downstream from source to mouth
We went to the river to have fun
questions.explain: A hypothesis is a precise, testable statement predicting a relationship (here, velocity vs distance downstream) that data can support or reject. The others are vague and not measurable.

questions.q: Why is careful PLANNING before a field trip important?
options: It removes the need to analyse results
It is not important; data can be collected randomly
It ensures suitable sites, methods and equipment are chosen so the data will be valid and safe to collect
It guarantees the hypothesis will be proved correct
questions.explain: Planning selects appropriate locations, methods, timing and equipment and considers safety, so the data collected will actually test the hypothesis reliably.

questions.q: Which is an example of PRIMARY data?
options: Measurements of river depth you took yourself in the field
A census table downloaded from a government website
A rainfall graph copied from a textbook
questions.explain: Primary data is collected first-hand by the investigator during fieldwork. The others are secondary data, gathered by someone else.

questions.q: Which statement about SECONDARY data is correct?
options: It is data collected by someone else, e.g. from maps, censuses or websites
It is always more reliable than primary data
It can only be collected in the field
It is the same as a hypothesis
questions.explain: Secondary data comes from existing sources such as OS maps, government statistics, weather records and published studies, rather than being measured first-hand.

questions.q: A student uses old census data AND their own street survey. What are these, respectively?
questions.explain: The census data was collected by others (secondary) while the student's own survey is collected first-hand (primary). Using both strengthens an enquiry.

questions.q: In RANDOM sampling...
options: Measurements are taken at fixed, regular intervals
Only the most convenient points are chosen
Every point has an equal chance of being selected, e.g. using random numbers
Samples are chosen to match the proportions of sub-groups
questions.explain: Random sampling gives every location or person an equal chance of selection (e.g. random number grid references), reducing bias.

questions.q: SYSTEMATIC sampling means...
options: Taking measurements at regular intervals, e.g. every 10 metres
Only sampling where it is easiest
Choosing points to reflect group proportions
questions.explain: Systematic sampling collects data at fixed regular intervals (every 10 m, every 5th person), giving even coverage that is easy to organise.

questions.q: A town's population is 60% adults and 40% under-18s. To reflect this in a questionnaire, which sampling method should be used?
questions.explain: Stratified sampling divides the population into groups (strata) and samples each in proportion, so the sample mirrors the real make-up of the population.

questions.q: Which technique measures the SPEED of a river?
options: A flow meter or a float timed over a set distance
questions.explain: River velocity is measured with a flow meter, or by timing a float over a measured distance (distance ÷ time = velocity).

questions.q: To investigate whether a beach's pebbles get smaller along the shore, you should measure...
options: Pebble long-axis length and roundness at points along the beach
questions.explain: Longshore drift is tested by measuring pebble size (long-axis) and roundness at intervals along the beach, using calipers/a ruler and a roundness chart.

questions.q: An 'environmental quality survey' (EQS) in an urban study is used to...
options: Score features such as litter, noise, greenery and building condition using a rating scale (a bipolar survey)
questions.explain: An EQS uses a rating/bipolar scale to score environmental features (e.g. cleanliness, greenery, upkeep) so that different locations can be compared.

questions.q: A well-designed QUESTIONNAIRE should mainly avoid...
options: Leading or biased questions that push respondents towards an answer
questions.explain: Leading questions bias results. Good questionnaires use clear, mostly closed questions, are short, and are asked of a fair sample of people.

questions.q: Which presentation method is most suitable for showing how ONE variable changes continuously along a river's course?
options: A choropleth of the whole country
questions.explain: A line graph clearly shows how a variable (e.g. width or velocity) changes continuously with distance downstream, revealing the trend.

questions.q: You want to show pedestrian counts AT different survey points on a town map. Which technique fits best?
options: A scatter graph with no location
Located (proportional) bars or symbols placed on the map
A single pie chart with no map
questions.explain: Located or proportional symbols/bars placed on a base map show both the value and its geographical location, ideal for point data across an area.

questions.q: What does GIS stand for, and what is it used for in fieldwork?
options: Geographic(al) Information System; storing, mapping and analysing spatial data
questions.explain: A Geographical Information System layers and maps spatial data, letting students display and analyse where patterns occur (e.g. mapping their results digitally).

questions.q: During ANALYSIS of results, a student should mainly...
options: Describe patterns and trends in the data and explain why they occur, linking back to the hypothesis
Only describe what happened on the trip
questions.explain: Analysis identifies and describes patterns/trends, notes anomalies, and explains them using geographical understanding, relating findings back to the hypothesis.

questions.q: A valid CONCLUSION to an enquiry should...
options: Only describe how much fun the trip was
State whether the hypothesis is supported or rejected, using evidence from the results
questions.explain: The conclusion directly answers the original question/hypothesis, saying whether the evidence supports or rejects it and summarising the key findings.

questions.q: A good EVALUATION of fieldwork should include...
options: A copy of the raw data table
Recognising limitations and sources of error, and suggesting how the investigation could be improved
questions.explain: Evaluation reflects on reliability and accuracy: it identifies weaknesses (small sample, weather, human error) and suggests realistic improvements.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a RISK ASSESSMENT before fieldwork?
options: To decide the best graphs to draw
To identify possible hazards and plan how to reduce or avoid them so fieldwork is carried out safely
questions.explain: A risk assessment identifies hazards (e.g. slippery riverbanks, traffic, weather), judges the risk and sets out control measures to keep everyone safe.
